1.title: Know blog words and readers
1.intro: A blog is a website with posts. Start with the basic words and the people you write for.
pts: Learn the terms: post, page, topic, domain, hosting, draft, publish, link, audience.
A niche is a topic you can write about for a long time.
Name one reader in one line: who they are, what they need, what worries them.
Read five blogs and list the topic, reader and how often they post.
1.ex: Niche: 'cheap healthy lunches for students'. Reader: a student with a small budget and 20 minutes.
1.act: Read five blogs and fill a table of topic, reader and post count. Write your niche in one line.
1.std: Task: study five blogs. Condition: public pages only. Standard: table complete and niche fits one line.

2.title: Explain how a post goes from idea to published
2.intro: A post follows steps. If you can name them, you can write on a schedule.
pts: The steps: idea, outline, draft, edit, check facts, add image, publish, share.
An outline lists the title, three to five headings and the one point of each.
Keep a list of ten ideas and choose one per week.
Set a fixed day each week to publish.
2.ex: Idea: 'five lunches under five dollars'. Outline: intro, five lunches, shopping list, summary.
2.act: Write an outline for three posts and a four-week calendar.
2.std: Task: plan four weeks. Condition: with one post a week. Standard: each post has a title, outline and date.

3.title: Write and publish a clear post
3.intro: Now you apply the basics. Write a post that is clear, true and easy to scan.
pts: Put the main point in the first two sentences.
Use short words, short paragraphs and clear headings.
Use your own photos or free-to-use images and say where they came from.
Read aloud and cut every word that does nothing.
3.ex: Before: 'Many people consider lunch an important meal.' After: 'A good lunch costs less than five dollars. Here are five.'
3.act: Write and publish your first 500-word post. Edit it twice.
3.std: Task: publish one post. Condition: using a free blog tool. Standard: one clear point, own words, image source noted, no spelling errors.

4.title: Follow Canadian rules for blogs
4.intro: Canada has rules for copyright, honest ads, privacy and email. Learn which touch your blog.
pts: Copyright: do not copy other people's text or images without permission; quote briefly and say the source.
If you are paid or get a free product to write, tell readers clearly. Advertising must be truthful.
Collecting emails or using visitor data falls under privacy law; add a plain privacy page and ask consent.
Sending commercial email needs consent and an unsubscribe link; check the current anti-spam rules.
4.ex: A brand sends you a free pan. Your post says at the top: 'I received this pan for free.'
4.act: Make a table of rule, what you must do and where you checked for ten situations.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: from official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unclear cases say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Understand costs and ways to earn
5.intro: A blog can earn money slowly. Learn the costs and the income types.
pts: Costs: domain name, hosting, email tool, image tool, your time.
Ways to earn: ads, affiliate links, your own products, paid services, sponsorship.
Earnings depend on visitors and trust, not only on posts.
Blog income is business income in Canada; keep records and check tax rules with the tax agency.
5.ex: 1,000 visitors a month, 2 percent buy a 15 USD guide: 20 sales, 300 USD. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Build a one-page budget and an income forecast for six months.
5.std: Task: make a forecast. Condition: with simple spreadsheet. Standard: costs, income types and visitor assumptions all stated.

6.title: Find readers and grow
6.intro: Readers find you through search, sharing and email. Build a steady way to be found.
pts: Write titles that match what people type into a search box.
Link between your own posts and to reliable sources.
Share on one or two social places where your readers are.
Offer a simple email sign-up with consent and track the numbers.
6.ex: Title 'How to meal-prep lunches for a week' matches a real search. A post titled 'Lunch ideas' is too vague.
6.act: Publish four posts in a month and track visits, sign-ups and shares.
6.std: Task: grow readers. Condition: with real posts and a free analytics tool. Standard: numbers logged weekly and one lesson written.

7.title: Protect your readers, your work and your accounts
7.intro: A professional blogger protects privacy, ownership and sign-ins.
pts: Use strong unique passwords and two-step sign-in.
Back up posts and images every month.
Do not share personal details about other people without consent.
Check facts, names and links before publishing, and fix errors openly.
7.ex: A reader points out a wrong price. You fix it and add: 'Updated: price corrected.'
7.act: Write a privacy page, a one-page content policy and a monthly backup checklist.
7.std: Task: write three documents. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: each is in plain words and dated.

8.title: Run a real pilot and decide
8.intro: Now you run it for real. Publish, measure and decide how to grow.
pts: Set a 60-day goal, such as eight posts and 500 visitors.
Every week record posts, visitors, sign-ups and time spent.
Ask five readers what they liked and what to change.
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
8.ex: After 60 days: 8 posts, 620 visitors, 25 sign-ups. You decide to focus on the two posts that drew most readers.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the weekly log and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real posts and real readers. Standard: log complete, decision uses numbers, a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What is a niche?
A topic you can write about for a long time for a clear reader.
What are the steps of a post?
Idea, outline, draft, edit, check, image, publish, share.
Why put the main point first?
Readers scan and may leave early.
What must you say if you get a free product?
Tell readers clearly that you received it.
What do commercial emails need?
Consent, a clear sender and an unsubscribe link.
Name three ways a blog can earn.
Ads, affiliate links, own products, services or sponsorship.
Why back up your blog?
To recover your work if the site or account fails.
What do you do with a wrong fact?
Fix it openly and note the update.
Why use free-to-use images?
Copying images without permission breaks copyright.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
